# Weekly Book Topics 50Q - week of 13 Sep 2026 (Mon 14 - Sat 19 Sep)

*Auto-generated for UPSC CSE 2027 prep. Feeds the website's Sectional practice flow. Static book-topic set, not current affairs.*

## Week focus

**Basis:** the **Sunday Sweep dated 2026-09-13**, which plans **Sun 13 Sep -> Sat 19 Sep 2026** - the upcoming week after this Sunday run - and sits in the **second half of F8** (8-21 Sep). Sunday is revision-only under the now-settled Sunday rule, so all new reading falls in **Mon 14 - Sat 19 Sep**, and this set tests those six days.

The Sweep's own Sunday row is explicit about how to use this file: run the Book-topics 50Q **"against Laxmikanth Ch 50 (Panchayati Raj) as a cold pre-read diagnostic"** - attempt it *before* reading the chapter, mark what you don't know, and let Monday's reading answer it. The set is weighted accordingly and then covers the rest of the week's static reading in proportion to the hours the Sweep allots it.

| Block | Source | Q | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Polity - Panchayati Raj** | Laxmikanth **Ch 50** + the 73rd Amendment text | Q1-12 | Monday's full two-hour block, the densest chapter in the Local Government part, and the Sweep's named pre-read target. Articles 243-243-O, the Eleventh Schedule, the committee ladder, and above all the **compulsory-vs-voluntary** split that Prelims lives on. |
| **Polity - Municipalities** | Laxmikanth **Ch 51** | Q13-19 | Thursday's second hour. Part IXA, Arts 243P-243ZG, the Twelfth Schedule, the three types of municipality, and the DPC/MPC pair that is almost always tested on its fractions. |
| **Polity - UTs, Scheduled and Tribal Areas** | Laxmikanth **Ch 52-53** | Q20-27 | Friday's second hour, read as one block because both are exceptions to the uniform constitutional scheme. Arts 239-241, 239AA, 240, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, and PESA 1996. |

**No repeats, and the one near-repeat is declared.** The last six book-topics sets (26 Jul, 02 Aug x2, 09 Aug x2, 11 Aug, 16 Aug, 23 Aug, 30 Aug, 06 Sep) closed Polity through the **Union** institutions, the constitutional bodies and then the **State Government** tier (Laxmikanth Ch 10-49), Vivek Singh through Ch 14 including Land Reforms, Spectrum through the British-rule thematics, physical and human Geography (NCERT-11 complete, NCERT-12 Ch 1-6), Shankar Ch 3-8, space / nuclear / defence / biotechnology, Art & Culture Ch 1, Ancient through the Mauryas, and IR with the US, China, Russia and the Nepal-Bhutan-Bangladesh file.

This week's Polity block is a clean advance - **one tier below the State**, into Part IX and Part IXA, which have never appeared in a book-topics set. Economy, Ancient and Geography all advance by chapter with no overlap. The only area with prior coverage is **Space Technology**, tested on 16 Aug; it is therefore cut from nine questions to **one**, and that one is restricted to the institutional layer the earlier set left untouched. This is an advance, not a revision round.

**Verification note.** Facts that are either date-sensitive or commonly misstated in coaching material were web-checked before use rather than written from memory:

- **Q17** - the two planning-committee fractions were verified against the bare text: **not less than four-fifths** elected for the **District** Planning Committee (Art 243ZD) and **not less than two-thirds** for the **Metropolitan** Planning Committee (Art 243ZE), which has a **ten lakh** population threshold. Coaching notes swap these two constantly.
- **Q21** - Article 240's operative list was checked against the bare text. The question is written around the *nature* of the power (a regulation may repeal or amend an Act of Parliament; the power ceases for Puducherry from the first meeting of its Legislature) and **deliberately avoids asserting the exact list of covered Union Territories**, because printed sources disagree on whether Ladakh has been added to the Article 240 list and the bare text retrieved does not confirm it.
- **Q24 and Q26** - Tribes Advisory Council: **not more than twenty members, three-fourths from the ST MLAs** of the State. Autonomous District Council: **not more than thirty members, four nominated by the Governor and twenty-six elected**, elected members for five years, nominated members at the Governor's pleasure.
- **Q27** - PESA was enacted on **24 December 1996** on the recommendations of the **Dilip Singh Bhuria** Committee under **Art 243M(4)(b)**, and it speaks of the Gram Sabha's **recommendation** for **minor** minerals and its **consultation** on land acquisition - not consent, and not major minerals.
- **Q29** - National MPI: **NITI Aayog**, **Alkire-Foster** dual-cutoff method, **three** equally weighted dimensions, **twelve** SDG-aligned indicators.
- **Q34** - the **Nutrient Based Subsidy** scheme took effect **1 April 2010** for P&K fertilisers; urea remains under statutory MRP outside NBS; the recommended **N:P:K** application ratio is **4:2:1**.
- **Q37** - the "Indo-Greeks issued the first gold coins in India" line that appears in several textbooks is **not safe as stated**, so the question is built the other way round: the Indo-Greeks are credited with the first coins definitely attributable to named kings (portrait + legend), and substantial gold coinage *within India* is attributed to the Kushanas. The explanation says so explicitly.
- **Q38, Q39** - Heliodorus pillar: ambassador of **Antialcidas** to **Bhagabhadra**, Garuda pillar to **Vasudeva** (*devadeva*), in **Brahmi**. Junagadh: **Rudradaman I**, a **Saka Western Kshatrapa** (not a Kushana), c. 150 CE, repair of the **Sudarshana** lake originally built under **Chandragupta Maurya**.

**Nothing in this set is claimed to be a verbatim UPSC PYQ.** The stems follow UPSC's statement-based, pair-matching, how-many-are-correct and single-best-answer patterns, but all fifty are newly written. No question depends on a current-affairs item: the live hooks the Sweep lists for this week (draft Art 371(K) for Ladakh, the FRA Gram Sabha consent question, PMAY-U 2.0, the SCE-200 hot test) are deliberately **excluded from the stems**, because a cold pre-read diagnostic should test the chapter, not the news.

## How to use

**Attempt this cold, before Monday's reading - that is the whole point of it this week.** One sitting, **60 minutes**, no notes, mark and move. Do not look anything up mid-paper.

Then debrief in two passes. First, the usual two categories only: **wrong answers** and **lucky guesses**, one line each on *why the wrong statement is wrong* rather than which option was right. Second, and specific to a pre-read diagnostic: take every Polity item you got wrong in Q1-12 and write its article number at the top of Monday's blank notebook page **before** you open Laxmikanth. Read the chapter looking for those answers. That converts a bad score into a reading plan, which is the only reason to sit a paper on material you have not studied.

**Benchmark, adjusted for the cold attempt.** The Easy set (15 Q) should still be near-perfect where it draws on Economy, Geography and History - those you have read. The Polity Easy items you have *not* read yet, so treat a miss there as information, not failure. What matters is the gap between Q1-27 (unread) and Q28-50 (read): if the read blocks are not clearly stronger, the problem is retention of last week's material, not this week's chapter. Difficulty mix is **15 Easy / 25 Moderate / 10 Hard**. Re-take blind on Thursday, once Ch 50 and Ch 51 are done, and again the following Sunday before the F8 close-out on Mon 21 Sep.

## Questions


### Polity - Panchayati Raj (Laxmikanth Ch 50)

**1.** With reference to Part IX of the Constitution, consider the following statements:
1. It was inserted by the Constitution (73rd Amendment) Act, 1992 and comprises Articles 243 to 243-O.  
2. It came into force on 24 April 1993.  
3. The 73rd Amendment also added the Eleventh Schedule, containing 29 functional items.  
Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1 and 2 only  
(b) 2 and 3 only  
(c) 1 and 3 only  
(d) 1, 2 and 3  

**2.** Under Part IX of the Constitution, the 'Gram Sabha' consists of:

(a) all persons ordinarily resident in a village, irrespective of age  
(b) persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to a village comprised within the area of a Panchayat at the village level  
(c) the elected members of the Panchayat at the village level together with the Sarpanch  
(d) the heads of all households in a village, as determined by the State Government  

**3.** Consider the following statements regarding the evolution of Panchayati Raj in India:
1. The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended a three-tier structure, and the scheme was first inaugurated in Rajasthan in 1959.  
2. The Ashok Mehta Committee recommended a two-tier structure with the mandal panchayat as the base.  
3. The L.M. Singhvi Committee recommended that Panchayati Raj institutions be given constitutional recognition.  
4. The Constitution (64th Amendment) Bill, 1989 was passed by both Houses of Parliament but was later struck down by the Supreme Court.  
Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1, 2 and 3 only  
(b) 2 and 4 only  
(c) 1, 3 and 4 only  
(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4  

**4.** Consider the following statements:
1. Article 243B requires Panchayats to be constituted at the village, intermediate and district levels in every State without exception.  
2. A State whose population does not exceed twenty lakh may choose not to constitute Panchayats at the intermediate level.  
3. On the commencement of Part IX, the 29 subjects of the Eleventh Schedule stand automatically transferred to the Panchayats.  
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?  

(a) 1 only  
(b) 2 only  
(c) 2 and 3 only  
(d) 1 and 3 only  

**5.** Under Article 243C, the Chairperson of a Panchayat at the intermediate level is:

(a) elected directly by the voters of the intermediate area  
(b) elected by and from amongst the elected members of that Panchayat  
(c) nominated by the State Government from amongst the elected members  
(d) the Block Development Officer, ex officio  

**6.** With reference to the reservation of seats for women in Panchayats under Article 243D, which one of the following statements is correct?

(a) It shall not be less than one-third of the total number of seats to be filled by direct election, and this one-third includes the seats reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes  
(b) It is one-third of the seats remaining after reservation for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes has been made  
(c) It shall not be less than one-half of the total number of seats, following the 2009 constitutional amendment  
(d) It is entirely a matter for State legislation, the Constitution merely recommending one-third  

**7.** Consider the following statements about the duration of Panchayats under Article 243E:
1. Every Panchayat shall continue for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting, unless dissolved earlier.  
2. An election to constitute a Panchayat shall be completed before the expiry of its duration, or within six months of the date of its dissolution.  
3. A Panchayat constituted upon the dissolution of a Panchayat before the expiration of its full term shall itself continue for a full term of five years.  
Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1 and 2 only  
(b) 2 and 3 only  
(c) 1 and 3 only  
(d) 1, 2 and 3  

**8.** The minimum age prescribed by the Constitution for a person to be qualified to contest an election to a Panchayat is:

(a) 18 years  
(b) 21 years  
(c) 25 years  
(d) 30 years  

**9.** With reference to the conduct of Panchayat elections, consider the following statements:
1. The State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor.  
2. He shall not be removed from office except in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of a High Court.  
3. His conditions of service shall not be varied to his disadvantage after his appointment.  
4. The superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for Panchayat elections vests in the Election Commission of India.  
Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1 and 4 only  
(b) 2, 3 and 4 only  
(c) 1, 2 and 3 only  
(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4  

**10.** Which of the following are compulsory provisions of Part IX of the Constitution, as distinct from provisions left to the discretion of the State Legislature?
1. Reservation of seats for backward classes in Panchayats  
2. Constitution of a Finance Commission by the State every five years to review the financial position of the Panchayats  
3. Representation of Members of the Legislative Assembly in Panchayats at the district level  
4. Audit of the accounts of Panchayats  
Select the correct answer using the code given below:  

(a) 1 and 3 only  
(b) 2 and 4 only  
(c) 1, 2 and 4 only  
(d) 2, 3 and 4 only  

**11.** Consider the following statements regarding Article 243M:
1. Part IX does not apply to the Scheduled Areas and the tribal areas referred to in Article 244.  
2. Part IX does not apply to the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram.  
3. Parliament may, by law, extend the provisions of Part IX to the Scheduled Areas and tribal areas, subject to such exceptions and modifications as it may specify.  
4. Any such law of Parliament extending Part IX to the Scheduled Areas shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368.  
Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1, 2 and 3 only  
(b) 3 and 4 only  
(c) 1 and 2 only  
(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4  

**12.** Article 243-O of the Constitution provides that:

(a) no election to any Panchayat shall be called in question except by an election petition presented to such authority and in such manner as provided by the State Legislature  
(b) the validity of any law relating to the delimitation of constituencies for Panchayat elections may be questioned in any court  
(c) all Panchayat electoral disputes shall lie directly before the Supreme Court under Article 32  
(d) the High Court shall have exclusive original jurisdiction over all disputes concerning Panchayat elections

(b) 2 and 3 only  
(c) 1 and 2 only

(a) a smaller urban area  
(b) a transitional area, that is, an area in transition from a rural area to an urban area

(a) Nagar Panchayat  
(b) Municipal Council  
(c) Municipal Corporation

**16.** The constitution of Wards Committees is mandatory in every municipality having a population of:

(a) one lakh or more

(c) three lakh or more  
(d) five lakh or more  

**17.** Consider the following statements about planning committees under Part IXA:
1. A District Planning Committee is constituted at the district level in every State to consolidate the plans prepared by the Panchayats and the Municipalities in the district.  
2. At least two-thirds of the members of a District Planning Committee are elected by and from amongst the elected members of the district panchayat and the municipalities in the district.

Select the correct answer using the code given below:  

(a) 1 only  
(b) 1 and 2 only  
(c) 2 and 3 only  
(d) 1, 2 and 3  

**19.** With reference to the composition of Municipalities under Article 243R, consider the following statements:
1. All the seats in a Municipality shall be filled by persons chosen by direct election from the territorial constituencies, known as wards.  
2. The State Legislature may provide for the representation in a Municipality of persons having special knowledge or experience in municipal administration, and such persons shall not have the right to vote in the meetings of the Municipality.  
3. The Chairperson of a Municipality shall in all cases be elected directly by the voters of the municipal area.  
Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1 and 3 only  
(b) 2 and 3 only

(d) 1, 2 and 3

### Economy - Inclusive Growth and Subsidies (Vivek Singh Ch 8-9)

**28.** With reference to the Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient, consider the following statements:
1. The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of the population.  
2. The greater the area between the Lorenz curve and the line of perfect equality, the higher the Gini coefficient.  
3. A Gini coefficient of zero indicates perfect inequality.  
Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1 and 3 only  
(b) 1 and 2 only  
(c) 2 and 3 only  
(d) 1, 2 and 3  

**29.** With reference to India's National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), consider the following statements:
1. It is constructed by NITI Aayog using the Alkire-Foster methodology.  
2. It measures simultaneous deprivation across three equally weighted dimensions - health, education and standard of living.  
3. It uses twelve indicators aligned to the Sustainable Development Goals.  
4. It has replaced the consumption-expenditure-based poverty line for determining household entitlements under the National Food Security Act.  
Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1, 2 and 3 only  
(b) 2 and 4 only  
(c) 1 and 3 only  
(d) 1, 2, 3 and 4  

**30.** With reference to official poverty estimation in India, consider the following statements:
1. The Tendulkar Committee moved away from an exclusively calorie-anchored poverty line to a basket that explicitly included private expenditure on health and education.  
2. The Rangarajan Committee recommended a higher poverty line than the Tendulkar line, and consequently produced a higher estimate of the poverty ratio.  
3. The Rangarajan Committee's poverty line was formally adopted by the Government as the official poverty line of India.  
Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1 and 3 only  
(b) 2 and 3 only  
(c) 1 and 2 only  
(d) 1, 2 and 3

### Ancient History - Post-Mauryan India and the Sangam Age (TN Class 11)

**36.** The Sunga dynasty, which succeeded the Mauryas in Magadha, was founded by:

(a) Pushyamitra Sunga  
(b) Agnimitra  
(c) Devabhuti  
(d) Vasudeva Kanva  

**37.** With reference to the Indo-Greeks, consider the following statements:
1. They were the first rulers in India to issue coins that can be definitely attributed to named kings, bearing the king's portrait and name.  
2. Menander, known in Indian tradition as Milinda, is the interlocutor of the Buddhist text Milindapanha, a dialogue with the monk Nagasena.

Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1 and 3 only  
(b) 2 and 3 only  
(c) 1 and 2 only  
(d) 1, 2 and 3  

**38.** With reference to the Heliodorus pillar inscription at Besnagar (Vidisha), consider the following statements:
1. It was set up by a Greek ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas at the court of the Sunga ruler Bhagabhadra.  
2. It records the erection of a Garuda pillar in honour of Vasudeva, described as the God of gods.  
3. It is written in the Brahmi script.  
Which of the statements given above are correct?  

(a) 1 and 2 only  
(b) 2 and 3 only  
(c) 1 and 3 only

## Answer key with explanations

**1.** **(d)** 1, 2 and 3 *[Easy - 73rd Amendment Act 1992 - Part IX, Articles 243-243-O, Eleventh Schedule]*

All three are correct. The 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 added Part IX ('The Panchayats'), Articles 243 to 243-O, and the Eleventh Schedule with 29 functional items. It received Presidential assent on 20 April 1993 and came into force on 24 April 1993, now observed as National Panchayati Raj Day. Note the contrast to remember: the Eleventh Schedule has 29 items (panchayats), the Twelfth has 18 (municipalities).

**2.** **(b)** persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to a village comprised within the area of a Panchayat at the village level *[Easy - Gram Sabha - Articles 243(b) and 243A]*

Article 243(b) defines the Gram Sabha as a body consisting of persons registered in the electoral rolls relating to a village comprised within the area of a Panchayat at the village level. Article 243A makes the Gram Sabha a compulsory provision, but leaves its powers and functions to be determined by the State Legislature - which is precisely why the Gram Sabha's real strength varies so widely across States, and why PESA, 1996 had to specifically empower it in Scheduled Areas.

**3.** **(a)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Moderate - Committees on Panchayati Raj - Balwant Rai Mehta, Ashok Mehta, G.V.K. Rao, L.M. Singhvi; 64th Amendment Bill]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended 'democratic decentralisation' through a three-tier system; Rajasthan inaugurated it at Nagaur on 2 October 1959. The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977) proposed a two-tier system - zila parishad and mandal panchayat. The L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986) is the one that asked for constitutional status and for the Gram Sabha as the base of decentralised democracy. Statement 4 is wrong: the 64th Amendment Bill, 1989 (Rajiv Gandhi government) was passed by the Lok Sabha but was defeated in the Rajya Sabha - it never became law, so there was nothing for a court to strike down.

**4.** **(b)** 2 only *[Moderate - Article 243B three-tier structure and the 20 lakh exception; Article 243G devolution]*

Only statement 2 is correct. Article 243B does mandate a three-tier system, but it carries an express exception: a State having a population not exceeding twenty lakh need not constitute Panchayats at the intermediate level - so statement 1's 'without exception' makes it wrong. Statement 3 is the single most important conceptual trap in this chapter: the Eleventh Schedule is a *list*, not a *transfer*. Article 243G empowers - but does not compel - the State Legislature to endow Panchayats with such powers and authority as may be necessary, and to devolve any of those 29 subjects. This is why devolution stalled: the funds, functions and functionaries all remain with the State unless it chooses otherwise.

**5.** **(b)** elected by and from amongst the elected members of that Panchayat *[Moderate - Article 243C - direct election of seats, indirect election of chairpersons]*

Article 243C provides that all seats in a Panchayat at every level are filled by direct election from territorial constituencies, but the Chairpersons at the intermediate and district levels are elected *indirectly* - by and from amongst the elected members of the respective Panchayat. Only at the village level is the manner of electing the Chairperson left to the State Legislature (which is why some States directly elect the Sarpanch and others do not). The distinction to hold: seats are always directly elected; chairpersonships above the village level never are.

**6.** **(a)** It shall not be less than one-third of the total number of seats to be filled by direct election, and this one-third includes the seats reserved for women belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes *[Easy - Article 243D - reservation of seats, women's one-third floor]*

Article 243D(3) reserves not less than one-third of the total number of seats to be filled by direct election for women, and Article 243D(2) requires that not less than one-third of the seats reserved for SCs and STs be reserved for women of those categories - i.e. the women's quota is a fraction *of the total*, inclusive of the SC/ST reserved seats, not an add-on. Option (c) is a common confusion: the proposal to raise the quota to one-half has been implemented by several States through their own laws, but the constitutional floor remains one-third. Option (d) is wrong because reservation for women is a compulsory provision; reservation for backward classes is the voluntary one.

**7.** **(a)** 1 and 2 only *[Moderate - Article 243E - five-year term, six-month election rule, remainder-of-term principle]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Statement 3 is wrong and is the classic trap: a Panchayat constituted after a premature dissolution continues only for the *remainder* of the period for which the dissolved Panchayat would have continued. There is a further rider worth memorising: no such fresh election need be held at all where the remainder of the term is less than six months. The design principle is that the five-year cycle itself is protected, not the tenure of any particular body - which is what makes dissolution a much weaker weapon in the State's hands than it looks.

**8.** **(b)** 21 years *[Easy - Article 243F - disqualifications, minimum age 21]*

Article 243F provides that a person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of a Panchayat if he is less than 21 years of age - even though the voting age is 18. Otherwise, the disqualifications are those applicable under any law for elections to the State Legislature, and all questions of disqualification are referred to such authority as the State Legislature may provide. Contrast the thresholds: 21 for a Panchayat or Municipality, 25 for the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly, 30 for the Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Council.

**9.** **(c)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Moderate - Article 243K - State Election Commission, appointment by Governor, removal like a High Court judge]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct; statement 4 is wrong. Article 243K vests the superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all Panchayat elections in a *State* Election Commission, consisting of a State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor. The removal protection - same manner and same grounds as a High Court judge - and the bar on varying his service conditions to his disadvantage are the two provisions that make the office genuinely independent, and they are worth pairing with Article 243K's counterpart for municipalities, Article 243ZA, which uses the same body. The Election Commission of India has no role in local body elections.

**10.** **(b)** 2 and 4 only *[Hard - Compulsory versus voluntary provisions of Part IX]*

Only 2 and 4 are compulsory. Article 243-I requires the Governor to constitute a State Finance Commission at the expiration of every fifth year, and Article 243J requires the State Legislature to make provision for the maintenance and audit of Panchayat accounts. Items 1 and 3 are voluntary: reservation for backward classes (Article 243D(6)) and representation of MPs and MLAs in Panchayats (Article 243C(3)) are both phrased as powers the State Legislature 'may' exercise. The compulsory/voluntary split is the highest-yielding distinction in this chapter - the compulsory list runs to Gram Sabha, three-tier structure, direct elections, SC/ST and women's reservation, five-year term with six-month elections, age 21, State Finance Commission, audit, State Election Commission and the bar on judicial interference in electoral matters.

**11.** **(a)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Hard - Article 243M - exemptions from Part IX and Parliament's extension power]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Article 243M exempts the Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas and Sixth Schedule tribal areas, the States of Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram, the hill areas of Manipur having a district council, and the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council areas of West Bengal in respect of that Council's functions. Article 243M(4)(b) is the door through which Parliament walked to enact PESA, 1996. Statement 4 is wrong - and this is the discriminating detail: the proviso expressly says no such law shall be deemed to be an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368, which is exactly why PESA is an ordinary Central Act passed by simple majority rather than a constitutional amendment.

**12.** **(a)** no election to any Panchayat shall be called in question except by an election petition presented to such authority and in such manner as provided by the State Legislature *[Easy - Article 243-O - bar to interference by courts in electoral matters]*

Article 243-O bars interference by courts in electoral matters relating to Panchayats: the validity of any law relating to the delimitation of constituencies or the allotment of seats cannot be called in question in any court, and no election to a Panchayat can be questioned except by an election petition presented to the authority and in the manner provided by State law. Option (b) states the exact opposite of the provision. Article 243ZG is the mirror provision for municipalities - the two are worth learning as a pair, since they are the only articles in Parts IX and IXA that limit judicial review.

**13.** **(d)** 1, 2 and 3 *[Easy - 74th Amendment Act 1992 - Part IXA, Articles 243P-243ZG, Twelfth Schedule]*

All three are correct. The 74th Amendment Act, 1992 added Part IXA ('The Municipalities'), Articles 243P to 243ZG, and the Twelfth Schedule with 18 functional items, and came into force on 1 June 1993 - about five weeks after its Panchayat twin. Keep the four numbers paired and they stop getting confused: 73rd / Part IX / Eleventh Schedule / 29 items / 24 April 1993, against 74th / Part IXA / Twelfth Schedule / 18 items / 1 June 1993.

**14.** **(b)** a transitional area, that is, an area in transition from a rural area to an urban area *[Moderate - Article 243Q - three types of municipalities]*

Article 243Q provides for three types of municipalities by size and character: a Nagar Panchayat for a transitional area (in transition from rural to urban), a Municipal Council for a smaller urban area, and a Municipal Corporation for a larger urban area. The Governor specifies what counts as each, having regard to population, density, revenue generated for local administration, the percentage of employment in non-agricultural activities and economic importance. A metropolitan area (population of ten lakh or more) is a separate concept used for the Metropolitan Planning Committee under Article 243ZE, not a fourth type of municipality.

**15.** **(d)** Cantonment Board *[Easy - Bodies outside Part IXA - cantonment boards, notified area committees, industrial townships]*

Part IXA recognises only three types of municipality - Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council and Municipal Corporation. A Cantonment Board is set up by the Central Government under the Cantonments Act for civilian populations in military stations and is administered by the Ministry of Defence; it falls outside Part IXA altogether. The other urban bodies that are also *not* municipalities and are worth listing once: notified area committees, town area committees, townships, port trusts and special purpose agencies such as development authorities. Article 243Q also allows the Governor to dispense with a municipality entirely in an 'industrial township' where municipal services are provided by an industrial establishment.

**16.** **(c)** three lakh or more *[Moderate - Article 243S - Wards Committees, three lakh threshold]*

Article 243S makes Wards Committees compulsory only in municipalities with a population of three lakh or more, each consisting of one or more wards within the territorial area of the municipality. The State Legislature decides their composition, territorial extent and how seats in them are filled. Keep the three population thresholds in Parts IX and IXA distinct: twenty lakh (a State may skip the intermediate Panchayat tier, Article 243B), three lakh (Wards Committee compulsory, Article 243S) and ten lakh (metropolitan area, hence a Metropolitan Planning Committee, Article 243ZE).

**17.** **(a)** 1 and 3 only *[Hard - Articles 243ZD and 243ZE - District and Metropolitan Planning Committees, four-fifths versus two-thirds]*

Only 1 and 3 are correct - statements 2 and 4 have the two fractions swapped, which is exactly how this pair is tested. Article 243ZD requires that not less than **four-fifths** of the members of a District Planning Committee be elected from amongst the elected members of the district panchayat and the municipalities, in proportion to the rural-urban population ratio. Article 243ZE requires that not less than **two-thirds** of the members of a Metropolitan Planning Committee be elected from amongst the elected members of the municipalities and the chairpersons of the panchayats in the metropolitan area, in proportion to their populations. A useful mnemonic: the smaller unit (district) carries the larger fraction.

**18.** **(b)** 1 and 2 only *[Easy - Institutions shared between Part IX and Part IXA - Articles 243-I/243Y and 243K/243ZA]*

Items 1 and 2 are shared. Article 243-I constitutes the State Finance Commission for Panchayats, and Article 243Y provides that the same Commission shall also review the financial position of Municipalities. Likewise Article 243K constitutes the State Election Commission, and Article 243ZA provides that elections to Municipalities shall be conducted by that same Commission. The Metropolitan Planning Committee (Article 243ZE) exists only in Part IXA, as does the District Planning Committee (Article 243ZD) - though the DPC's *function* is to consolidate both panchayat and municipal plans.

**19.** **(c)** 1 and 2 only *[Moderate - Article 243R - composition of Municipalities, non-voting nominated members]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 243R fills all municipal seats by direct election from wards, and permits the State Legislature to provide for the representation of persons with special knowledge or experience in municipal administration - expressly *without* the right to vote in meetings - as well as for MPs, MLAs and the chairpersons of committees. Statement 3 is wrong: the manner of electing the Chairperson of a Municipality is left entirely to the State Legislature, which is why some States have a directly elected mayor and others elect the mayor from among the councillors. Compare Article 243C, where the Chairpersons at the intermediate and district Panchayat levels *must* be elected indirectly.

**20.** **(a)** Article 239 *[Easy - Article 239 - administration of Union Territories, Governor as Administrator]*

Article 239(1) places the administration of every Union Territory in the President, acting through an Administrator appointed by him with such designation as he may specify - Lieutenant Governor, Chief Commissioner or Administrator. Article 239(2) adds a point regularly tested: the President may appoint the Governor of a State as the Administrator of an adjoining Union Territory, and where he does so, the Governor exercises those functions independently of his Council of Ministers. The neighbouring articles are worth fixing alongside: 239A (a local legislature and Council of Ministers for a UT, by Parliamentary law), 240 (President's regulation-making power) and 241 (High Courts for UTs).

**21.** **(d)** 1, 2 and 3 *[Moderate - Article 240 - President's regulation-making power and the Puducherry proviso]*

All three are correct. Article 240 empowers the President to make regulations for the peace, progress and good government of the Union Territories that do not have a legislature; such a regulation may repeal or amend any Act of Parliament or other law applicable to the territory, and once promulgated it has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament applying there. The proviso in Article 240(1) is the detail that carries the question: once a body is created under Article 239A to function as a Legislature for Puducherry, the President shall make no such regulation with effect from the date appointed for that Legislature's first meeting - the power revives only if the Legislature is dissolved or its functioning remains suspended.

**22.** **(c)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Moderate - Article 239AA - special provisions for Delhi, 69th Amendment 1991, excluded entries]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The 69th Amendment Act, 1991 inserted Articles 239AA and 239AB, designating Delhi the National Capital Territory with a Legislative Assembly and a Council of Ministers. Article 239AA(3)(a) excludes from the Assembly's competence Entries 1 (public order), 2 (police) and 18 (land) of the State List, along with Entries 64, 65 and 66 so far as they relate to Entry 18. Statement 4 is wrong, and statement 3 shows why: the Lieutenant Governor acts on ministerial advice *except* in matters where he is required to act in his discretion, and in case of a difference of opinion he refers the matter to the President, acting in the meantime at his own discretion in an urgent case. Article 239AB provides for the suspension of these provisions, i.e. President's rule in Delhi.

**23.** **(a)** Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram *[Easy - Article 244 - Fifth Schedule versus Sixth Schedule coverage]*

Article 244(1) applies the Fifth Schedule to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in any State other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram - and those four are precisely the States whose tribal areas are governed instead by the Sixth Schedule under Article 244(2). Option (c) names four States that actually *have* Fifth Schedule areas. The President declares an area to be a Scheduled Area, and may alter, increase, decrease or rescind such designation, in consultation with the Governor of the State concerned.

**24.** **(b)** 1 and 2 only *[Moderate - Fifth Schedule - Tribes Advisory Council composition and advisory character]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Fifth Schedule requires a Tribes Advisory Council in each State having Scheduled Areas - and the President may also direct its establishment in a State having Scheduled Tribes but no Scheduled Areas. It has not more than twenty members, three-fourths of whom must be representatives of the Scheduled Tribes in the State Legislative Assembly (if there are fewer such representatives, the remaining seats are filled by other members of those tribes). Statement 3 is wrong: the Council only *advises* on matters referred to it by the Governor. That advisory-only character is the core weakness of the Fifth Schedule model, and the sharpest contrast with the Sixth Schedule's Autonomous District Councils, which actually legislate.

**25.** **(a)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Hard - Fifth Schedule - Governor's powers, President's assent, report to the President]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct; statement 4 reverses the position. Paragraph 5 of the Fifth Schedule gives the Governor the power to exclude or modify the application of Central and State laws in a Scheduled Area, and the power to make regulations - including regulations prohibiting or restricting the transfer of land by or among Scheduled Tribes, regulating money-lending, and regulating the allotment of land - which may repeal or amend an existing law but require the President's assent. Paragraph 3 requires the Governor's report to the President, and expressly provides that the executive power of the Union *does* extend to giving directions to the State as to the administration of those areas. Note too that the Governor must consult the Tribes Advisory Council before making such regulations.

**26.** **(c)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Moderate - Sixth Schedule - autonomous district councils, composition, applicable States]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. An autonomous district council under the Sixth Schedule has not more than thirty members - four nominated by the Governor and twenty-six elected on adult franchise - with the elected members serving five years and the nominated members holding office at the Governor's pleasure. Statement 4 is wrong: the four States are Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and **Mizoram**, not Nagaland (Nagaland instead has its own special provision, Article 371A). Hold the contrast in one sentence: the Fifth Schedule is executive protection administered through the Governor; the Sixth Schedule is devolved self-government through elected councils with legislative, judicial and financial powers.

**27.** **(b)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Hard - PESA 1996 - Gram Sabha powers, consultation versus consent, minor minerals]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. PESA, enacted on 24 December 1996 on the recommendations of the Dilip Singh Bhuria Committee and using the power in Article 243M(4)(b), extends Part IX to the Fifth Schedule areas with the Gram Sabha as the operative unit - competent to safeguard community resources, own minor forest produce, prevent the alienation of land and restore unlawfully alienated land, and to be consulted on land acquisition and resettlement. Statement 4 fails on two counts, and both matter: PESA speaks of the *recommendation* of the Gram Sabha, not its consent, and it covers **minor** minerals - the grant of concessions for major minerals is outside its scope. The consultation-versus-consent gap is the single most litigated weakness in PESA's design, and it is the standard answer to 'why has PESA underdelivered?'

**28.** **(b)** 1 and 2 only *[Easy - Measuring inequality - Lorenz curve, Gini coefficient, Palma ratio]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Lorenz curve plots cumulative income share against cumulative population share, ranked from poorest to richest; the 45-degree diagonal is the line of perfect equality. The Gini coefficient is the ratio of the area between the Lorenz curve and that diagonal to the total area beneath the diagonal, so a curve that sags further from the diagonal yields a higher Gini. Statement 3 inverts the scale: Gini runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality). Note the Gini's known blind spot, which is why the Palma ratio - the income share of the top 10 per cent divided by that of the bottom 40 per cent - is often reported alongside it: the Gini is most sensitive to changes in the middle of the distribution, where least of the policy interest lies.

**29.** **(a)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Moderate - National MPI - Alkire-Foster method, three dimensions, twelve indicators]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The National MPI, published by NITI Aayog, applies the Alkire-Foster dual-cutoff counting method (the same method underlying the global MPI of OPHI and UNDP) across three equally weighted dimensions captured by twelve SDG-aligned indicators - health (nutrition, child and adolescent mortality, maternal health), education (years of schooling, school attendance) and standard of living (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets, bank account). Statement 4 is wrong: the MPI is a monitoring and diagnostic instrument, not an entitlement-determining one; NFSA coverage is still fixed by the statutory ceilings and State-wise allocations worked out from Census population. The honest limitation to remember is that the National MPI is computed from the National Family Health Survey, so its reference years lag.

**30.** **(c)** 1 and 2 only *[Moderate - Poverty estimation - Tendulkar and Rangarajan Committees]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Tendulkar Committee (report 2009) abandoned the calorie-norm anchor that had descended from the 1979 Task Force, shifted to a uniform all-India reference basket, moved to Mixed Reference Period consumption data, and priced in private spending on health and education. The Rangarajan Committee (2014) set a higher line - both rural and urban - and therefore counted more people as poor than the Tendulkar methodology did for the same year. Statement 3 is wrong: the Rangarajan report was submitted but its recommendations were not accepted, which is why the Tendulkar line remained the last officially used series and why India has had no fresh official poverty ratio since. That vacuum is exactly the gap the National MPI and the 2022-23 Household Consumption Expenditure Survey are now being read into.

**31.** **(b)** revenue expenditure *[Easy - Subsidies as revenue expenditure; revenue versus capital expenditure]*

Subsidies are revenue expenditure: they neither create physical or financial assets nor reduce a liability of the government. This classification is the hinge of the entire fiscal critique of the subsidy bill - because a large and rising share of revenue expenditure in total expenditure means a correspondingly smaller share available for capital expenditure, which is what actually adds to the economy's productive capacity. It also explains why subsidies bear directly on the revenue deficit and, through the effective revenue deficit, on the FRBM consolidation path, and why off-budget or extra-budgetary financing of subsidy arrears - repeatedly flagged by the CAG - understates the true position.

**32.** **(c)** 1 and 2 only *[Moderate - Explicit versus implicit subsidies; merit versus non-merit goods]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The explicit/implicit distinction is about *visibility in the accounts*: an explicit subsidy is a budgeted cash outgo, while an implicit subsidy is the unrecovered cost of a service furnished below economic cost - irrigation water, electricity supplied by a State utility, higher education at subsidised fees. The merit/non-merit distinction is about *economic justification*: merit goods generate positive externalities so that private consumption falls short of the social optimum, which is the market-failure case for subsidising them. Statement 3 confuses the two axes - they are independent. A non-merit subsidy can be perfectly explicit (the fertiliser subsidy is budgeted and is classed as non-merit), and a merit subsidy can be implicit. Getting these two axes straight is what lets you argue both sides in a Mains answer.

**33.** **(b)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Hard - Food subsidy - FCI economic cost, Central Issue Price, MSP-CIP wedge]*

The economic cost is the sum of the MSP (the pooled cost of grain), procurement incidentals such as mandi charges, commission, bagging, transport and levies, and distribution costs including freight, storage, interest and handling losses. The Central Issue Price is not a component of cost at all - it is the price the FCI *recovers* from beneficiaries under the NFSA. The food subsidy is precisely the wedge: economic cost minus the CIP realisation, multiplied by the quantity issued. Because the CIP has been effectively frozen since 2013 while MSP and carrying costs have risen every year, the subsidy grows even when the quantum of grain distributed does not - which is the structural point behind every proposal to revise NFSA coverage or index the CIP.

**34.** **(d)** 1, 2 and 3 *[Moderate - Fertiliser subsidy - NBS 2010, urea statutory MRP, N:P:K imbalance]*

All three are correct. The NBS scheme came into effect on 1 April 2010, replacing product-based subsidy for non-urea fertilisers with a fixed per-nutrient subsidy on N, P, K and S, leaving the MRP of P&K fertilisers to be set by manufacturers. Urea was deliberately kept out and continues under statutory price control at a notified MRP. The consequence is the central paradox of the regime: because urea's price barely moved while P&K prices rose several-fold after 2010, farmers substituted towards urea, pushing actual application ratios well away from the agronomically recommended N:P:K of 4:2:1 and degrading soil health. Neem-coating of urea (mandated 2015) targets diversion to industry rather than the imbalance; PM-PRANAM, approved in 2023, tries to address the imbalance directly by incentivising States to reduce chemical fertiliser use.

**35.** **(c)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Hard - Petroleum subsidy deregulation, PAHAL, DBT - leakage versus exclusion error]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. Petrol prices were deregulated in June 2010 and diesel in October 2014, since when both have been market-determined at the retail level. PAHAL (the relaunched DBTL) converts the LPG subsidy into a cash transfer: the consumer pays the market price and receives the subsidy in the bank account - the textbook case of shifting from a price subsidy to an income transfer, which removes the incentive to divert. Statement 3 states the honest limit of DBT, and it is the point examiners reward: DBT is an excellent instrument against *inclusion* error and diversion, and no instrument at all against *exclusion* error - a genuinely poor household missing from the database, or failing biometric authentication, is excluded more cleanly than before. Statement 4 is wrong: PMUY provides deposit-free LPG connections with support for the first refill and stove, not a cash transfer in lieu of cylinders.

**36.** **(a)** Pushyamitra Sunga *[Easy - Sungas - Pushyamitra, Bharhut and Sanchi, the persecution narrative]*

Pushyamitra Sunga, a general of the last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha, founded the dynasty around 185 BCE. Agnimitra was his son and successor - the hero of Kalidasa's *Malavikagnimitram* - and Devabhuti was the last Sunga ruler, assassinated by his minister Vasudeva, who founded the short-lived Kanva dynasty. The Sunga period is art-historically important out of proportion to its politics: the Bharhut stupa railing and the gateway and railing additions at Sanchi belong to it. One caveat worth carrying into an answer: the standard narrative of Pushyamitra as a persecutor of Buddhism rests largely on later Buddhist texts such as the *Divyavadana*, and the archaeological record of continued stupa patronage in his period sits awkwardly with it.

**37.** **(c)** 1 and 2 only *[Moderate - Indo-Greeks - portrait coinage, Menander and the Milindapanha, gold coinage]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Indo-Greek issues are the first coins in India that can be assigned with certainty to individual kings, because they carry both the royal portrait and the ruler's name in legend - everything earlier, the punch-marked silver, is anonymous. Menander (c. 165-145 BCE) is the Milinda of the *Milindapanha*, 'The Questions of Milinda', recording his exchange with the monk Nagasena. Statement 3 reverses the sequence, and this is the trap: substantial gold coinage *in India* begins with the Kushanas - Vima Kadphises and Kanishka I - not the Indo-Greeks, whose gold issues belong largely to the Bactrian side of their realm. Textbook formulations that credit the Indo-Greeks with 'the first gold coins in India' should be read with that qualification.

**38.** **(d)** 1, 2 and 3 *[Moderate - Heliodorus pillar - Antialcidas, Bhagabhadra, Garuda pillar to Vasudeva]*

All three are correct. Heliodorus, son of Dion, was the ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas of Taxila to the court of Bhagabhadra, and the pillar he erected at Besnagar near Vidisha is a Garuda-dhvaja dedicated to Vasudeva (Krishna), styled *devadeva*, the God of gods; the inscription is in Prakrit in the Brahmi script. It is the single most useful artefact for two separate exam themes: it is early epigraphic evidence for the Bhagavata/Vaishnava cult, and it is the best documented case of a Greek official adopting an Indian devotional form - a genuine two-way cultural interaction rather than a one-directional 'Greek influence'.

**39.** **(c)** 1, 2 and 3 only *[Moderate - Junagadh inscription - Rudradaman I, Saka Western Kshatrapas, Sanskrit epigraphy]*

Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Junagadh (Girnar) rock inscription of about 150 CE is a landmark in Indian epigraphy because it is among the earliest substantial records in polished literary Sanskrit, at a time when Prakrit still dominated inscriptional use. It records the repair of the Sudarshana lake after a storm breached its embankment - and, usefully for chronology, it tells us the lake was built by Pushyagupta, a provincial governor under Chandragupta Maurya, and improved by Tushaspha under Ashoka. Statement 4 is wrong: Rudradaman I was a Saka ruler of the Western Kshatrapa line, a contemporary and rival of the Satavahanas, not a Kushana. The same rock, incidentally, also carries Ashokan edicts and a later Skandagupta inscription - three dynasties on one surface.

**40.** **(d)** 1, 2 and 3 *[Moderate - Kushanas - Saka era 78 CE, Fourth Buddhist Council, the Kushana court]*

All three are correct. The era commencing 78 CE - adopted in 1957 as the basis of the Indian national calendar - is conventionally, though not unanimously, taken to have been founded by Kanishka I. The Fourth Buddhist Council at Kundalavana in Kashmir was presided over by Vasumitra with Ashvaghosha as vice-president, and it is the council at which the Mahayana-Hinayana division hardened and the *Mahavibhasha* commentaries were compiled. The Kushana court set worth memorising as a group is Ashvaghosha (author of the *Buddhacharita*), Nagarjuna (the Madhyamika philosopher of *sunyata*), Charaka (medicine) and Vasumitra. The dynastic sequence to hold alongside it: Kujula Kadphises, then Vima Kadphises (who begins the substantial gold coinage), then Kanishka I.

**41.** **(c)** Only three *[Hard - Post-Mauryan art - Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati schools]*

Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correct; pair 4 is not. Gandhara sculpture is carved chiefly in grey schist (and later stucco), shows unmistakable Greco-Roman modelling - wavy hair, a halo, heavy naturalistic drapery - and conveys spiritual calm through realistic bodily form, so the description in pair 4 contradicts pair 1 on every count. Mathura works in the distinctive spotted red sandstone of Sikri, in a robust indigenous idiom, and is the one school of the three that sculpted Jaina tirthankaras and Brahmanical deities alongside Buddhist images. Amaravati, on the lower Krishna under Satavahana patronage, works in a white limestone or marble-like stone and is distinguished above all by its crowded narrative relief medallions. On the vexed question of which school produced the first Buddha image, the defensible position is that Gandhara and Mathura developed anthropomorphic Buddha images at broadly the same time, independently.

**42.** **(a)** 1, 2 and 4 only *[Moderate - Satavahanas - Prakrit, metronymics, coinage, Nashik prashasti, land grants]*

Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The Satavahanas used Prakrit written in Brahmi for their records - the Naneghat inscriptions of Naganika and the Nashik cave prashasti issued by the queen-mother Gautami Balashri in praise of her son Gautamiputra Satakarni are the standard examples - and the dynasty is unusual in Indian history for its metronymics (Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra), which point to a patriarchal succession combined with the social prominence of the mother's lineage. Statement 3 is wrong: Satavahana coinage is predominantly lead, potin, copper and some silver, reflecting the Deccan's metal availability; gold coinage on a large scale belongs to the Kushanas and later the Guptas. Also worth carrying forward: the Satavahanas were the first Indian rulers to make recorded land grants, tax-free, to Brahmanas and Buddhist monks - the institutional seed of the later *agrahara* and of medieval land-grant economy.

**43.** **(c)** 1, 2 and 4 only *[Hard - Sangam age - Tolkappiyam, corpus structure, post-Sangam epics, the tinai scheme]*

Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. The *Tolkappiyam*, attributed to Tolkappiyar, is the earliest extant Tamil work on grammar and poetics and the framework within which the rest of the corpus is read. The *Tirukkural* of Tiruvalluvar is counted among the Pathinenkilkanakku or Eighteen Minor Works. The *tinai* scheme - the fivefold classification by landscape into kurinji (hills), mullai (pastoral forest), marutam (riverine cropland), neytal (littoral) and palai (arid) - is the most exam-productive single concept in Sangam literature, because each zone carries its own deity, occupation, flora and emotional register. Statement 3 is wrong: the *Silappadikaram* of Ilango Adigal and the *Manimekalai* of Sattanar are the twin epics generally assigned to the *post*-Sangam period, later than the Ettuthogai (Eight Anthologies) and Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls) that form the core corpus. For the trade context, the *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea*, Pliny's complaint about the drain of Roman gold, and the Roman coin hoards and amphorae at Arikamedu are the evidence to cite.

**44.** **(d)** 1, 2 and 3 *[Easy - Coal - Gondwana versus Tertiary deposits, Damodar valley coalfields]*

All three are correct. Gondwana coal, roughly 200 million years old, accounts for the overwhelming majority of India's reserves and all of its metallurgical-grade coal; the principal fields lie in the Damodar valley (Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro, Giridih, Karanpura) and in the Godavari, Mahanadi, Son and Wardha valleys. Tertiary coal, about 55 million years old and typically higher in sulphur and moisture, is found in Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland, with lignite - brown coal of tertiary age - concentrated at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu. The exam-relevant consequence of statement 1: India's coking-coal deficit is structural, which is why steel capacity remains import-dependent even though total coal output is large.

**45.** **(b)** 1 and 3 only *[Moderate - The three mineral belts of India and their coal endowment]*

Statements 1 and 3 are correct. NCERT groups India's mineral occurrences into three broad belts. The north-eastern plateau belt - the Chotanagpur plateau and the Odisha plateau, spanning Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal - is the richest, combining iron ore, manganese, mica, bauxite, chromite and the Gondwana coalfields, which is why India's heavy industry clustered there. The north-western belt along the Aravallis in Rajasthan and Gujarat is associated with non-ferrous metals such as copper, lead and zinc, plus sandstone, gypsum and the Gujarat petroleum and natural gas fields, and it has no coal. Statement 2 is wrong: the south-western plateau belt of Karnataka and Goa is rich in iron ore and manganese and in ferrous metals generally, but it is *deficient* in coal except for lignite at Neyveli in the adjacent region - the belt's iron-ore wealth was historically exported rather than smelted locally for exactly that reason.

**46.** **(b)** the beach sands of Kerala and Tamil Nadu *[Easy - Monazite and thorium - beach sands; the three-stage nuclear programme]*

Monazite, a phosphate mineral carrying thorium and rare earths, occurs in the monazite-rich beach and placer sands of the Kerala and Tamil Nadu coasts, with further occurrences in Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. This is the resource endowment on which the third stage of Homi Bhabha's three-stage nuclear programme rests: stage one uses natural uranium in pressurised heavy water reactors, stage two burns the plutonium so produced in fast breeder reactors while breeding U-233 from a thorium blanket, and stage three runs thorium-U-233 reactors. Thorium is not itself fissile - Th-232 is fertile and must be converted to U-233 - which is why the third stage is the last, not the first, and why India's uranium constraint is not solved simply by holding large thorium reserves.

**47.** **(d)** 1, 2 and 3 *[Moderate - Industrial regions, location factors, the sugar industry's southward shift]*

All three are correct. The Hugli region, the oldest industrial belt in the country, grew around jute processing along the river, aided by Kolkata port, Raniganj coal and cheap migrant labour from the eastern plains. The sugar industry's southward shift is the standard NCERT illustration of raw-material orientation: peninsular cane has higher sucrose content, the crushing season is longer, and the cooperative sector is stronger, so Maharashtra overtook Uttar Pradesh in output even though UP retains the larger cane area. The Chotanagpur cluster - Jamshedpur, Bokaro, Durgapur, Rourkela, Burnpur - is the classic weight-losing, raw-material-oriented location in the Weberian sense: coal, iron ore, manganese, limestone and water lie within a short radius. The policy layer to attach: the National Logistics Policy, 2022 and the industrial-corridor programme are aimed precisely at loosening these inherited location constraints by cutting logistics cost as a share of GDP.

**48.** **(d)** 1, 2 and 3 *[Moderate - India-Sri Lanka - 1987 Accord, Thirteenth Amendment, IPKF, Katchatheevu]*

All three are correct. The Indo-Sri Lanka Accord of July 1987, signed by Rajiv Gandhi and J.R. Jayewardene, led to the Thirteenth Amendment, which created the provincial council system and made Tamil an official language - and the full implementation of that Amendment, particularly its devolution of land and police powers, has been India's consistent public ask ever since. The Accord also provided for the Indian Peace Keeping Force, whose deployment from 1987 to 1990 is a case study best treated candidly, as an intervention that turned into combat against the very group it was meant to disarm. The 1974 agreement placed Katchatheevu within Sri Lankan waters, and the associated fishing-rights question in the Palk Bay remains the most persistent irritant in the relationship, alongside the Trincomalee oil tank farm and grid-interconnection projects on the cooperative side of the ledger.

**49.** **(c)** Only three *[Hard - Neighbourhood connectivity projects - Maldives, Myanmar, Afghanistan]*

Pairs 1, 2 and 3 are correctly matched; pair 4 is not. The Greater Male Connectivity Project, India's largest infrastructure undertaking in the Maldives, links Male to Villingili, Gulhifalhu and Thilafushi. The Salma Dam on the Hari Rud in Herat province was inaugurated in 2016 and renamed the India-Afghanistan Friendship Dam. Sittwe is in Myanmar's Rakhine state, not Sri Lanka - it is the maritime terminus of the Kaladan project, which runs Kolkata to Sittwe by sea, up the Kaladan river to Paletwa, and then by road to Zorinpui on the Mizoram border. That corridor and the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway are the two reasons Myanmar's internal conflict is an Act East problem rather than only a neighbourhood one: India's entire land bridge to Southeast Asia runs through it. For the Maldives, the strategic fact to pair with the projects is location - the atolls straddle the Eight Degree and One and a Half Degree Channels, through which a large share of Indian Ocean commercial traffic passes.

**50.** **(c)** 1 and 2 only *[Moderate - IN-SPACe, NSIL and the Indian Space Policy 2023]*

Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre, IN-SPACe, is an autonomous single-window body under the Department of Space that authorises, promotes and supervises space activities by non-government entities, including their use of ISRO facilities. NewSpace India Limited, incorporated in 2019, is the commercial arm of the Department of Space and the successor in that role to Antrix. Statement 3 inverts the division of labour set out in the Indian Space Policy, 2023: the policy assigns *regulation and authorisation* to IN-SPACe and refocuses ISRO on research and development in advanced technologies, human spaceflight and planetary exploration while handing routine operational launch and satellite services progressively to industry through NSIL. ISRO is not the regulator and does not cease to do R&D - if anything the policy pushes it further towards R&D.


## Revision checklist

Twelve points. If you cannot do one of these from memory by Saturday night, the page is not built yet.

1. **The four paired numbers.** 73rd / Part IX / Eleventh Schedule / **29** items / in force **24 Apr 1993**, against 74th / Part IXA / Twelfth Schedule / **18** items / in force **1 Jun 1993**.
2. **The compulsory-vs-voluntary split of Part IX, written out in two columns.** Compulsory: Gram Sabha, three-tier (above 20 lakh), direct election of all seats, indirect election of intermediate/district chairpersons, SC/ST and one-third women's reservation, five-year term with six-month elections, age 21, State Finance Commission, audit, State Election Commission, bar on judicial interference. Voluntary: MP/MLA representation, backward-class reservation, devolution of the Eleventh Schedule, financial powers, the Gram Sabha's actual powers.
3. **Why devolution stalled, in one sentence per F:** funds, functions, functionaries - plus the parallel-body problem, and the fact that the **Eleventh Schedule is a list, not a transfer** (Art 243G).
4. **Art 243E's remainder rule** - a panchayat constituted after premature dissolution serves only the remainder, and no election is needed where the remainder is under six months.
5. **The three population thresholds**, and which article each sits in: **20 lakh** (intermediate tier optional, 243B), **3 lakh** (Wards Committee compulsory, 243S), **10 lakh** (metropolitan area, hence MPC, 243ZE).
6. **DPC four-fifths, MPC two-thirds** - said aloud, in that order, until swapping them becomes impossible.
7. **The four bodies that are NOT municipalities:** cantonment board, notified/town area committee, township, port trust and special purpose agencies - plus the Art 243Q **industrial township** exemption.
8. **Art 239AA's three excluded entries** - public order, police, land - and the LG's discretion plus reference to the President.
9. **Fifth vs Sixth Schedule in one sentence:** Fifth is executive protection administered through the **Governor** (TAC advisory, President's assent for regulations, annual report, Union may direct the State); Sixth is devolved self-government through **elected** Autonomous District Councils with legislative, judicial and financial powers. Plus the two State lists: Fifth applies **except** Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram; Sixth applies **to** exactly those four.
10. **PESA's two honest weaknesses:** *consultation*, not consent, on land acquisition; and *minor* minerals only. Pair with **Art 243M(4)(b)** and the proviso that such a law is **not** a constitutional amendment.
11. **The subsidy anatomy in three numbers:** FCI **economic cost** = MSP + procurement incidentals + distribution/carrying, and food subsidy = that minus **CIP** realisation; **NBS from 1 Apr 2010** for P&K with urea left under statutory MRP; recommended **N:P:K 4:2:1**. Then the DBT sentence: it fixes diversion and inclusion error, not **exclusion** error.
12. **The post-Mauryan spine in one line each:** Sungas (Bharhut, Sanchi railing) -> Indo-Greeks (portrait coins, Menander/Nagasena, Heliodorus pillar) -> Sakas (**Rudradaman I**, Junagadh, chaste Sanskrit, Sudarshana lake) -> Kushanas (**78 CE**, Fourth Council at Kundalavana under Vasumitra, Gandhara/Mathura) -> Satavahanas (Prakrit, metronymics, **first land grants**, Amaravati) -> Sangam (Tolkappiyam, Ettuthogai/Pattuppattu, the **five tinai**, Silappadikaram and Manimekalai as **post**-Sangam).
